creator: dailydoseofds_
caption: The next step after Karpathy's autoresearch idea 🧠  Tuning an agent is mostly manual work: editing prompts, tools, and control flow by hand, then rerunning evals to see what moved.  Researchers have been building automated optimizers to do that outer loop instead. The underlying process is the same: an LLM proposes a change, an evaluator scores it, and the proposer reads that result before proposing the next one.  They differ in what they edit and what feedback they get to read.  1️⃣ GEPA (Berkeley) - Optimizes the text of a system like prompts, tool descriptions, or the agent's own code. Instead of collapsing a run into one scalar reward the way RL does, it reads the full execution trace, diagnoses why the run failed, and proposes a targeted fix. Converges in hundreds of rollouts instead of the thousands GRPO needs.  2️⃣ AutoResearch (inspired by Karpathy) - Runs a narrower version of the loop where a coding agent iterates on a program.md file, scores outputs against fixed evals, and keeps whatever improves.  3️⃣ Meta-Harness - Points the loop at the harness itself, the scaffolding code that decides what to retrieve, how to format it, and what state to keep between calls.  The natural question is which one to use. The answer is none of them alone.  On the Frontier-CS benchmark, holding model, thinking effort, and budget fixed, no optimizer wins everywhere. Across 10 tasks, GEPA led on 3, AutoResearch on 3, and Meta-Harness on 4.  Each optimizer hill-climbs fast and then stalls. But handing the stalled candidate to a different optimizer breaks the plateau since each one attacks the problem differently.  omni (open-source) already automates all of that. It runs every optimizer on a fraction of the budget, takes the best candidate, and hands it to a fresh optimizer to keep going. It scores 7.8 percentage points above the best standalone optimizer at the same budget.  GitHub repo in the comments!  👉 Over to you: Which of the three optimizers would you start with?  #aiagents #optimization #ucberkeley

creator: damienbenveniste
caption: Boolean retrieval for AI agents becomes a different systems problem when a query is a graph rather than a tree. An agent can translate “find papers about gradient descent, exclude arXiv and deep learning” into strict logic, but the index still has to execute that logic without losing recall or exhausting memory.  Suppose a Boolean query computes the same sub-expression S in several places. In a directed acyclic graph, S is evaluated once and reused. A document-at-a-time engine usually runs a tree of stateful iterators, so the shared node cannot simply feed two parents. Unrolling the graph duplicates S, then duplicates everything below S. With enough reconvergence, the execution tree can grow exponentially.  Materializing every intermediate set avoids that duplication, but negation creates the opposite problem. For a toy universe U = {1, ..., 8}, let A = {2, 4, 6} and B = {4}. The query A AND NOT B should return {2, 6}. A naive materialized engine may first build NOT B = {1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8}, even though the useful operation is only A \ B.  One way around this trade-off is to change the representation. Keep each intermediate result as a small set of document IDs plus a POS or NEG flag. During intermediate evaluation, NOT B does not create U \ B; it leaves B = {4} and flips the flag to NEG. When A(POS) meets B(NEG), the AND operation becomes the sparse set difference A \ B = {2, 6}. Keep the original DAG and memoize S, so shared nodes are evaluated once and reused.  The boundary is important. If the overall query ends with a NEG root, finalization still has to materialize U minus the stored set. For Zero-Preserving queries, meaning they return nothing on an empty index, the root resolves POS. These include ordinary evidence-seeking requests such as A AND NOT B. In that case, exact constraints can be applied before ranking truncates the candidate set, while traversal stays tied to active posting lists rather than the whole document universe.

For Euclidean space \mathbb{R}^n,  \boxed{\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i y_i}  and the corresponding norm is  \boxed{\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}}.  A Hilbert space uses the same ideas of inner product, norm, orthogonality, projection, and basis, but also requires completeness: every Cauchy sequence must converge to a point inside the space.  So,  \boxed{\mathbb{R}^n \text{ is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space}}  while spaces such as  \boxed{L^2([a,b])}  provide important infinite-dimensional examples.  Hilbert spaces are fundamental in functional analysis, quantum mechanics, signal processing, Fourier analysis, PDEs, and control theory. caption: Why we jump to conclusions without realising it (ladder of inference)...  Ever been in a meeting where two people looked at the same data and saw completely different things?  That’s the Ladder of Inference in action, a model by Chris Argyris that explains how we move from observation to belief to action in seconds.  Here’s how it works.  We all climb a mental ladder (many times without realising it):  (1) Observable Data -- The raw facts. Sales dropped 10% this quarter.  (2) Selected Data -- What we choose to notice. We focus on one underperforming region, ignoring the rest.  (3) Added Meaning -- The story we tell yourself. “The regional manager isn’t pushing the team hard enough.”  (4) Assumptions -- The logic we fill in. “They’ve lost motivation.”  (5) Conclusions -- The judgment we form. “The region’s leadership is weak.”  (6) Beliefs -- The narrative that sticks. “That region is always a problem.”  (7) Actions -- The decisions we make. You cut their budget, morale drops, and performance gets worse, proving yourself “right.”  By breaking the line of thinking down we can see how we interpreted the facts and made faulty conclusions.  The Ladder of Inference shows how easily strategy meetings, team reviews, and client conversations go off track.  To use it well:  → Slow down your climb. Ask, “What did I actually observe?” → Test your assumptions. “Could there be another reason?” → Make your thinking visible. “Here’s how I got to this conclusion.” → Walk others down the ladder with you. “Let’s go back to what we both saw.”  Good strategy starts with clear thinking. creator: algoinsight
caption: Most engineers already use design patterns.  They just don’t know the names - which means they can’t search for the trade-offs.  CREATING 1. Singleton - one instance, shared 2. Factory Method - create without naming the class 3. Builder - assemble step by step  COMPOSING 4. Adapter - bridge two incompatible interfaces 5. Decorator - wrap to add behaviour 6. Facade - one door to a subsystem 7. Proxy - stand in front and control access 8. Composite - treat a leaf and a whole tree alike  COORDINATING 9. Observer - tell everyone on change 10. Strategy - swap the algorithm at runtime 11. Command - a request as an object 12. Iterator - walk it without exposing it 13. State - behave by current state 14. Template Method - skeleton, subclass fills in 15. Chain of Responsibility - pass it along until one handles it  Three things worth knowing:  1. Singleton is on every list and is the one to be MOST careful with. It’s global mutable state wearing a class: tests become order-dependent, dependencies hide from constructors, it bottlenecks under concurrency. Most uses really want “one instance managed by the container” - dependency injection, with the lifetime explicit and the object still swappable in a test.  2. Strategy and State are IDENTICAL on a class diagram and mean opposite things. Both delegate to an interchangeable object. The difference is who decides: with Strategy the CALLER picks, and strategies don’t know each other. With State the OBJECT transitions, and states know what comes next. If your “strategies” choose their own successor, you’ve written a state machine.  3. Decorator, Proxy and Adapter all wrap an object - only INTENT separates them. Decorator ADDS behaviour, same interface. Proxy CONTROLS access (lazy load, cache, permissions), same interface. Adapter CHANGES the interface so incompatible things can talk.  The point isn’t to use more patterns. It’s that “we need a Facade here” ends an argument that “we should wrap this somehow” can’t.  Which one did you write for years before learning it had a name? caption: Hierarchy of Mathematical Spaces 📐🧠  Mathematical spaces can be understood as layers of structure. We begin with a set, then add concepts such as topology, vector operations, inner products, norms, metrics, and completeness to create increasingly specialized spaces.  A typical progression is:  \text{Set} \rightarrow \text{Topological Space} \rightarrow \text{Vector Space} \rightarrow \text{Inner Product / Normed / Metric Structures} \rightarrow \text{Complete Spaces} \rightarrow \text{Hilbert Space} \rightarrow \text{Euclidean Space}  Each added structure gives us new mathematical tools: continuity, linear combinations, length, distance, angle, orthogonality, convergence, and completeness.  For example, a Hilbert space is a complete inner-product space, making it especially important in functional analysis, Fourier theory, quantum mechanics, and signal processing. Familiar finite-dimensional spaces such as \mathbb{R}^n with the usual dot product are Euclidean spaces.  One important point: these spaces do not always form a single strict chain—some relationships branch or require additional assumptions.  The hierarchy of mathematical spaces shows how adding structure transforms abstract collections into powerful frameworks for geometry, analysis, physics, and engineering.  #MathematicalSpaces #VectorSpace #TopologicalSpace #MetricSpace #NormedSpace #InnerProductSpace #HilbertSpace #EuclideanSpace #FunctionalAnalysis #LinearAlgebra #Mathematics #STEM #EEAnimation

creator: damienbenveniste
caption: Long-context on-policy distillation can reward a response for sounding teacher-like even when it misses the evidence the task actually requires. Token-level imitation and response-level success measure different things.  In on-policy distillation, the student generates its own answer, then a stronger teacher scores the generated tokens. If the teacher assigns a token more probability than the student did, that token receives a positive training signal. This gives dense feedback on states the student actually visits, instead of only on fixed reference outputs.  Consider a 50K-token contract task that requires six clauses. One rollout writes a fluent answer with five clauses. Another is awkward but includes all six. The first can look better token by token because every sentence is locally plausible. A verifier that checks coverage should prefer the second.  Group-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation, or GC-OPD, treats this as a disagreement problem. For a group of student rollouts, it computes:  residual = normalized verifier reward - normalized teacher score  If teacher and verifier rank a response similarly, the correction is small. If the teacher overrates an incomplete response, the residual is negative. If the verifier recognizes task completion that the teacher underweights, it is positive. Subtracting the teacher score matters because simply adding verifier reward can reinforce a preference the teacher already expressed.  The response-level residual still has to reach individual tokens. GC-OPD distributes it using bounded weights derived from each token's relative teacher advantage, while preserving the original dense distillation signal. Those weights allocate correction. They do not identify which token is objectively correct.  In one multi-table extraction diagnostic, pairwise teacher-verifier disagreement rose from 40.6% below 8K tokens to 64.0% at 32-64K. Across five long-context benchmarks, the Qwen3-8B average moved from 43.56 with vanilla OPD to 44.65 with GC-OPD under the same setup.

caption: The paddle in this animation cannot push a ball sideways. It can only choose where the ball lands on it. That is the hard part.  The concept is underactuation: you have fewer controls than the directions you need to move things. Most real machines are like this — a car can't slide sideways into a parking spot, and this paddle can't shove a ball left.  What you're watching: two balls fall under gravity onto one paddle that slides along a horizontal rail. The paddle's top is domed, not flat. At each contact the agent — the thing making decisions — picks two numbers: where on the rail to be, and how fast to strike upward.  That's it. Sideways aim is a side effect. Hit a ball off-centre on the dome and it reflects off at an angle, like a tennis ball off a shoulder rather than a racket face.  The score, the reward the agent learns to maximise, is simply how many catches in a row before a ball hits the floor. Two balls, one paddle, so every strike also has to buy time for the other ball.  Takeaway: when you're short an actuator, aim lives in geometry and timing, not in extra motors.  Reference: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics (MIT, underactuated.mit.edu); Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, for the reward-maximising setup.

caption: whoever leaked this has bigger balls than sense  SpaceXAI shipped five hireable workers for $200 a month, then wrote the catch into its own Grok Bot documentation and left the page up: all five run on one computer, so one sign-in hands the browser session, the files and the command-line credentials to every one of them  the NSA, CISA and the cyber agencies of the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand had published the opposite instruction 103 days earlier: no broad or unrestricted access, low-risk and non-sensitive work only  i ran four of mine on one account for a week, counting what each could reach: eleven signed-in apps, one browser profile, and deleting a bot left all of it standing  Grok Bot is worth hiring five times over, and you can draw its blast radius before the second one exists:  - sign in for the bot that needs the site, then open the others and see what they reach: that session is theirs the moment it exists - give each bot its own account on the app, since the docs tell you in writing to stop using separate bots as a security boundary - put the stop line in the description, as an approval controls the proposed action and leaves whatever already ran where it landed - cap the spend outside the product, because there is no bot-specific spend cap yet and the audit view of what they did is still coming - keep the money and the customer replies in your own hands, and let the other four start from scratch each morning on work that cannot bite  one sign-in is also why this pays: five names finish inside your real tools instead of handing you drafts to paste  my take, and it is the uncomfortable one: your real limit on Grok Bot is how many logins you will put on one machine, and the hiring was always the easy half #ai #fyp #softwaredevelopment #llm
